content: Down's syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 or a specific region of this chromosome. It is the most common congenital cause of intellectual disability and is associated with a range of metabolic and structural health issues. While some individuals with Down's syndrome may experience only mild challenges and lead relatively normal lives, others may face life-threatening complications or significant health problems. The birth of a child with Down's syndrome can have a profound impact on family dynamics and life. Noninvasive screening methods, such as biochemical analysis of maternal serum or urine and fetal ultrasound measurements, are used to estimate the likelihood of a pregnancy being affected by Down's syndrome. These tests provide information to guide decisions about further diagnostic testing, such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS). However, it is important to note that no screening test can predict the severity of the condition in an affected individual. The objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the accuracy of first-trimester serum markers for detecting Down's syndrome during pregnancy. The accuracy of these tests is measured by their sensitivity (the proportion of Down's syndrome cases correctly identified) and specificity (the proportion of unaffected pregnancies correctly identified as low risk). A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, BIOSIS, and others, up to August 25, 2011. Studies were included if they compared one or more screening tests to a reference standard, such as chromosomal verification or postnatal inspection. Both consecutive series and diagnostic case-control studies were eligible, as well as randomized trials comparing different screening strategies. Studies with fewer than five Down's syndrome cases or with more than 20% of participants lost to follow-up were excluded. Data were extracted to calculate detection rates (sensitivity) and false positive rates (1-specificity). The quality of the studies was assessed using the QUADAS criteria. Statistical analyses, including hierarchical summary ROC meta-analytical methods and random-effects logistic regression, were used to evaluate and compare test performance. A total of 56 studies, reported in 68 publications, were included in the review. These studies involved 204,759 pregnancies, of which 2,113 were affected by Down's syndrome. The studies were generally of good quality, although many relied on invasive testing only for high-risk pregnancies. A total of 78 test combinations, involving 18 different markers with or without maternal age, were evaluated. These markers included ADAM12, AFP, inhibin, PAPP-A, ITA, free βhCG, PlGF, SP1, total hCG, progesterone, uE3, GHBP, PGH, hyperglycosylated hCG, ProMBP, hPL, and ratios of free αhCG and free βhCG to AFP. Direct comparisons between two or more tests were made in 27 studies. Meta-analysis of the nine best-performing or most frequently evaluated test combinations showed that a strategy combining maternal age with the double markers PAPP-A and free βhCG was significantly more effective than using individual markers alone. This combination detected approximately seven out of every ten Down's syndrome pregnancies at a 5% false positive rate. Limited evidence suggested that marker combinations including PAPP-A might be more sensitive than those without it. The authors concluded that test strategies involving two markers, specifically PAPP-A and free βhCG, combined with maternal age, are significantly more accurate than single-marker strategies. These tests detect seven out of ten Down's syndrome pregnancies at a fixed 5% false positive rate. Adding additional markers (triple tests) has not been shown to provide statistically significant improvements, likely due to the small size and limited power of the included studies. The screening blood tests themselves pose no additional risks to the woman beyond those associated with a routine blood draw. However, women who receive a high risk screening result and subsequently undergo invasive diagnostic procedures, such as amniocentesis or CVS, face a risk of miscarriage, even if the baby is unaffected by Down's syndrome. Parents must carefully consider this risk when deciding whether to proceed with invasive testing following a high-risk screening result.
